exploratory.title: H1 without trial 1
exploratory.rationale: Checks whether the information-type effect on sharing depends on the first, possibly less attentive, trial.
exploratory.method: Re-fit the registered H1 specification (OLS, cluster by respondent, same covariates) on trials 2-4, one arm against True/neutral at a time.
exploratory.finding: The misinformation effect is -0.170 (SE 0.013) without trial 1, against -0.182 (SE 0.011) in the registered fit, so the result holds.

exploratory.title: Misinformation effect by age tertile
exploratory.rationale: Age is a demographic the PAP did not register, and it may change how much people penalise false content.
exploratory.method: Re-fit the registered H1 specification within each age tertile.
exploratory.finding: The misinformation penalty on sharing is -0.130 in the youngest tertile and -0.220 in the oldest, so older respondents share it less.

lit.text: The retrieved list is thin and mostly off-topic for these hypotheses. It contains no experimental or survey findings on how information type, tie strength, sharer trust, ideology, knowledge or conspiracy belief affect sharing or perceived plausibility of misinformation, so it cannot support or contextualize H1-H14, the reweighted robustness checks R1-R12, or the exploratory analyses X1-X13. The only directly relevant item is a general review of fake news, disinformation and misinformation on social media [citation removed: not in retrieved set], whose snippet gives no specific findings. A review of prejudice toward immigrants (Esses, 2020) is only loosely related to the sharer-origin hypotheses (H3, H10, X13). Its snippet reports no findings on how sharer origin affects information sharing or credibility, so I draw no conclusions from it.

takeaways: Headlines that were false or that corrected a false claim were shared less than true or neutral ones: misinformation by 18.2 points (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]), fact-checks by 13.3 points (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]).
Among the sharer attributes, which were measured and not randomized, a close tie raised sharing by 3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust in the sharer by 5.7 points (95% CI [2.3, 9.1]).
Sharer origin, political knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero for sharing, with intervals of roughly ±2 to ±4 points.

Registered subgroup comparisons show that respondents with high belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with low belief (p<0.001), and older respondents shared it 6.1 points less.
Many tests were run without correction, and the sharer attributes are measured ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive, not causal.
sections.abstract: This study asks how the type of information and the characteristics of the person sharing it shape whether people say they would share a post and how plausible they find it. In a registered conjoint experiment on a YouGov sample of US respondents (12,000 profiles, all analysed), each headline was randomly true or neutral, false, or a fact-check, and was attributed to one of the respondent's real contacts. Relative to true or neutral headlines, misinformation was 18.2 points less likely to be chosen for sharing (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]); plausibility showed a similar pattern. Close ties (+3.0 points) and highly trusted sharers (+5.7 points) raised sharing. Sharer origin, knowledge and belief in disputed claims were not distinguishable from zero. Respondents' own belief in disputed claims and their age moderated the response to misinformation. The sharer attributes are measured, not randomized, many tests were uncorrected, and several differences are small.
sections.design_notes: Each respondent rated pairs of posts, and the 12,000 profiles were all analysed; no rows were dropped for the main models, though a few outcome cells were missing by a handful of rows. Only the information type was randomized, with True/neutral headlines as the reference level (4,145 profiles with that level in the exploratory models). Tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are the respondent's own ratings of real contacts. Their effects are therefore descriptive contrasts that bundle correlated attributes. Standard errors are clustered by respondent. All tests labelled registered follow the AsPredicted plan; those labelled exploratory were specified after seeing the data.

results.H1: False headlines were chosen for sharing 18.2 points less often than true or neutral ones (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were 13.3 points lower (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1], p<0.001). Sharing rates were 60.3% for true or neutral headlines, 42.1% for misinformation and 47.0% for fact-checks. Because information type was randomized, these are causal estimates.
results.H2: Posts from close ties were chosen for sharing 3.0 points more often than those from distant ties (95% CI [1.0, 5.0], p=0.003, two-sided). Tie strength is a measured rating, so the contrast is descriptive.
results.H3: Posts from sharers in the continental US were not distinguishable from foreign-origin sharers in sharing (+0.2 points, 95% CI [−1.4, 1.8], p=0.81). The interval is narrow but still compatible with small effects either way.
results.H4: Moderate sharers were chosen 1.9 points less often than liberal sharers (95% CI [−3.7, −0.1], p=0.034), a result near the threshold given the many tests. Conservative sharers were −0.7 points (95% CI [−2.8, 1.5]), not distinguishable from liberal ones.
results.H5: Highly trusted sharers were chosen 5.7 points more often than low-trust sharers (95% CI [2.3, 9.1], p<0.001). Mid trust was +3.6 points (95% CI [−0.1, 7.3], p=0.056), not clearly distinguishable from zero.
results.H6: Sharer political knowledge was not distinguishable from zero for sharing: mid knowledge −0.0 points (95% CI [−2.0, 1.9]) and high knowledge +1.7 points (95% CI [−0.5, 3.9]), against low knowledge.
results.H7: High belief in disputed claims by the sharer was not distinguishable from low belief for sharing (−0.2 points, 95% CI [−1.9, 1.6], p=0.87).
results.H8: Misinformation was judged 18.6 points less often the more plausible post than true or neutral headlines (95% CI [−20.8, −16.4], p<0.001, two-sided). Fact-checks were 12.4 points lower (95% CI [−14.7, −10.2], p<0.001).
results.H9: Close ties raised plausibility by 2.8 points relative to distant ties (95% CI [0.7, 4.8], p=0.008).
results.H10: Sharer origin was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (−0.3 points, 95% CI [−1.9, 1.4]).
results.H11: Moderate sharers were rated 2.1 points less plausible than liberal sharers (95% CI [−4.0, −0.3], p=0.026), near the threshold. Conservative sharers were −1.9 points (95% CI [−4.1, 0.3]), not distinguishable from zero.
results.H12: Trust in the sharer was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility: mid −0.6 points (95% CI [−4.2, 3.0]) and high +2.5 points (95% CI [−0.7, 5.8]).
results.H13: Sharer political knowledge was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility; high knowledge was +1.7 points (95% CI [−0.4, 3.8]) and mid knowledge −0.1 points (95% CI [−2.1, 1.9]).
results.H14: The sharer's belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (−0.0 points, 95% CI [−1.8, 1.8], p=0.97).
results.RW: Re-weighting each source attribute by its inverse assignment probability left the picture essentially unchanged. For sharing, close ties stayed at +3.0 points (95% CI [1.0, 5.0]) and high trust rose slightly to +6.7 points (95% CI [3.3, 10.1]). The moderate-sharer contrast on sharing weakened to −1.7 points (95% CI [−3.5, 0.0], p=0.056). For plausibility, close ties (+2.7 points) and moderate sharers (−2.1 points) kept their sign and size. The remaining re-weighted estimates were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S1: Age moderated the response to information type. Among misinformation profiles, the oldest tertile shared 6.1 points less than the youngest (p<0.001). Differences for fact-checks (+3.0) and true or neutral headlines (+2.6) were not clearly distinguishable from zero. Most other levels showed little age difference.
results.S2: Respondent ideology mattered mainly for true or neutral headlines, which the most conservative tertile shared 5.6 points less than the most liberal (p=0.002). Continental-US sharers were also shared 1.6 points less by the conservative tertile (p=0.005), and liberal sharers 4.8 points less (p=0.017). Other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S3: Respondents with the highest belief in disputed claims shared misinformation 5.6 points more than those with the lowest (p<0.001), and true or neutral headlines 5.5 points less (p<0.001). They also shared posts from trusted sharers (−2.3 points), moderate sharers and continental-US sharers less. Fact-check differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S4: Respondents with high media trust shared misinformation 4.8 points more than those with low trust (p=0.003). Other differences were small, and the few at conventional significance, such as high-knowledge sharers (−2.4 points) and low-conspiracy sharers (+3.5 points), should be read cautiously given the many comparisons.
results.S5: Spanish-language respondents shared misinformation 3.6 points more than English-language respondents (p=0.010). Low-trust sharers (+7.9 points) and low-knowledge sharers (+3.2 points) were also shared more in Spanish; these rest on small cells. Most other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S6: For plausibility, the oldest tertile rated misinformation 4.0 points lower than the youngest (p=0.013) and liberal sharers 3.7 points higher (p=0.020). Other age differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S7: The most conservative respondents rated true or neutral headlines as less plausible by 4.9 points than the most liberal (p=0.006), and continental-US sharers by 1.5 points (p=0.009). Other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S8: Respondents with the highest belief in disputed claims rated misinformation as 6.8 points more plausible (p<0.001) and true or neutral headlines 6.9 points less (p<0.001). They also rated high-trust (−2.4 points) and high-knowledge (−3.6 points) sharers lower. Fact-check differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S9: High media trust was linked to rating misinformation 4.4 points more plausible (p=0.007), and posts from low-conspiracy sharers 4.4 points more plausible (p=0.009). High-knowledge sharers were rated 2.6 points lower (p=0.019). Most other differences were not distinguishable from zero.
results.S10: Spanish-language respondents rated misinformation as 3.7 points more plausible than English-language respondents (p=0.008). They also rated low-trust sharers 9.0 points higher and low-knowledge sharers 3.6 points higher, from small cells. The rest were not distinguishable from zero.
results.X1: Post hoc: each step up the 1-5 trust scale was linked to 1.4 points more sharing (SE 0.4, p<0.001). The slope was similar for misinformation (1.9 points) and fact-checks (1.7 points) and not clearly distinguishable from zero for true or neutral headlines (0.6 points).
results.X2: Post hoc: each step up the trust scale was linked to 1.3 points higher plausibility (SE 0.4, p<0.001). The slope was about 2 points for misinformation and fact-checks and about zero for true or neutral headlines.
results.X3: Post hoc: close ties raised sharing by 2.9 points (SE 1.0, p=0.006). The premium was 4.7 points for fact-checks and 3.5 for misinformation, but only 0.9 points for true or neutral headlines, which was not distinguishable from zero.
results.X4: Post hoc: among profiles chosen to share, misinformation was 5.5 points more likely to be shared while judged less plausible (95% CI [3.0, 8.1], p<0.001), 20.3% against 14.3% for true or neutral headlines. Fact-checks were +1.7 points (95% CI [−0.5, 4.0]).
results.X5: Post hoc: sharing was 4.4 points higher when respondent and sharer shared the same ideological lean than when they opposed (95% CI [0.9, 7.9], p=0.015). Pairs involving a moderate were +0.8 points (95% CI [−2.3, 3.9]).
results.X6: Post hoc: respondents whose contacts were seen as holding more disputed beliefs shared more misinformation, with a slope of 0.110 (SE 0.049, p=0.026, 3,196 profiles). This is a modest result among many tests.
results.X7: Post hoc: among partisan respondents, congenial content was shared 2.5 points more than uncongenial content, not distinguishable from zero (SE 1.9, p=0.18).
results.X8: Post hoc: across all headlines, the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero for sharing (slope 0.005, SE 0.014). It differs sharply by information type; see the within-type results.
results.X9: Post hoc: across all headlines, the sharer's perceived belief in disputed claims was not distinguishable from zero for plausibility (slope −0.005, SE 0.014).
results.X10: Post hoc and thin (266 profiles): the anti-vaccine headline was rated 16.5 points more plausible when the sharer was seen as believing the DNA claim (SE 6.7, p=0.013).
results.X11: Post hoc: the trust slope on sharing misinformation was 1.9 points per step across all misinformation (SE 0.8, p=0.013).
results.X12: Post hoc: the close-tie premium on sharing misinformation was 3.5 points (SE 1.7, p=0.040), near the threshold.
results.X13: Post hoc: sharer origin was not distinguishable from zero for sharing in the pooled origin-by-language-and-nativity check (0.2 points, SE 0.8, p=0.78).
results.XS1: Post hoc: the trust slope on sharing was 1.7 points for fact-checks, 1.9 for misinformation and 0.6 for true or neutral headlines. The differences between types were not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS2: Post hoc: the trust slope on plausibility was about 2 points per step for fact-checks and misinformation and about zero for true or neutral headlines. The gap to fact-checks was borderline (p=0.065).
results.XS3: Post hoc: the close-tie premium was 4.7 points for fact-checks, 3.5 for misinformation and 0.9 for true or neutral headlines. The gap between true or neutral headlines and fact-checks was borderline (p=0.050).
results.XS5: Post hoc: the gap between same-lean and opposed-lean sharers was 3.8 to 5.6 points across information types, with intervals including zero. The gaps did not differ clearly by type.
results.XS7: Post hoc: congenial misinformation was shared 5.4 points more than uncongenial (p=0.012), while fact-checks showed −0.2 points. The difference between them was 5.6 points (p=0.007).
results.XS8: Post hoc: a sharer perceived as believing disputed claims raised sharing of misinformation (slope 0.086, p=0.002) but not distinguishably of fact-checks (−0.044) or true or neutral headlines (−0.022). The gap with fact-checks was 0.131 (p=0.001).
results.XS9: Post hoc: the same pattern held for plausibility. The slope was +0.095 for misinformation (p<0.001) and negative for fact-checks and true or neutral headlines. The gap with fact-checks was 0.146 (p<0.001).
results.XS11: Post hoc: the trust slope for sharing misinformation was 2.5 points for health headlines (SE 2.0, 550 profiles) and 1.9 for political headlines. The difference was not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS12: Post hoc: the close-tie premium for misinformation was 0.7 points for health (SE 4.4) and 3.9 for political headlines (p=0.031). The difference was not distinguishable from zero.
results.XS13a: Post hoc: the sharer-origin slope on sharing was 0.4 points in English and 0.0 in Spanish. The difference was not distinguishable from zero (−0.5 points, SE 1.7).
results.XS13b: Post hoc: the sharer-origin slope was +1.3 points for foreign-born respondents and −0.8 for US-born respondents. The difference of −1.8 points (SE 1.6) was not distinguishable from zero.

exploratory.E1: Dropping the first trial gave a misinformation effect of −17.0 points (SE 1.3), against −18.2 in the registered fit. This unreviewed check agrees with the registered estimate.
exploratory.E2: In this unreviewed check, the misinformation penalty on sharing was −13.0 points in the youngest tertile and −22.0 in the oldest. Fact-check penalties stayed near −13 points in every tertile.

sections.limitations: Only information type was randomized. Tie strength, sharer origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are respondents' ratings of real contacts, so their effects are descriptive and bundle correlated traits. The design involves many tests across two outcomes, five registered moderators and a long list of subgroup contrasts, none corrected for multiplicity, so results near p=0.03 to 0.05 (for example the moderate-sharer contrast) deserve caution. Some cells are small, such as low-trust sharers and health headlines, and the Spanish-language contrasts rest on them. The outcome is a stated choice between two posts and not real sharing behaviour. The literature available here offered no benchmarks, so the effects are not placed against earlier work. The exploratory results are post hoc.
